headline: Monhegan Pollock, Eastern Egg Mackerel, and Bass Still Parked on the Bait
subhead: Warm water is keeping the bay's stripers content to sit on bunker instead of blitzing, but the groundfish and mackerel are making up for it in open water.
body_markdown:
Forty Septembers on this water teach you the same lesson every year before the calendar admits it: the first week of the month always looks like summer and fishes like a question mark. The water's still holding warm out past the islands, the bait's scattered instead of balled up, and the fish know a change is coming before anybody standing on a dock does. That's exactly where Penobscot Bay and the Midcoast sit right now — warm, restless, and not quite ready to tip over into the fall pattern everybody's waiting on.

The warm regime that's carried this whole summer offshore is still sitting on top of Gulf of Maine water, and it's showing up in strange ways — deep-drop swordfish gear working farther north than usual is one sign of it, and closer to home it means the striped bass are staged rather than committed. They're stacked around the river mouths — the Kennebec, the Sheepscot, the Damariscotta — sitting on schools of peanut bunker and pogies without the kind of tightly-wound blitz behavior that shows up once the nights turn cold. We flagged this pattern last week, calling for a gradual slide toward fall structure with no sudden turnover, and that's precisely what the bay's giving back. Nothing dramatic yet. The bass are there, they're just not in a hurry.

The moon's building toward full on the 6th and 7th, and that's worth watching closely over the next several days. Bigger tidal swings mean more current through the river mouths and the thoroughfares, and that current is what eventually organizes scattered bait into something a bass will commit to hard. Best window right now is the last two hours of the ebb at first light — slack water and bright sun just push these fish deeper and less interested. Eels fished on a fish-finder rig off Pemaquid Point and at the mouth of the Damariscotta have been drawing slot fish in the 28 to 34-inch range, and chunk bunker soaked on the bottom near the Sheepscot's ledges is picking off a few bigger stragglers after dark. Topwater at first light off the outer islands near Boothbay has produced some fish too, but it's a short window before the sun gets up and shuts it down.

Bluefish are the one thing that hasn't slowed a bit. Warm water's kept them aggressive and spread wide all summer, and that's held true straight through the last week — we said it would carry through Labor Day week, and the reports off Damariscove and the outer ledges near Boothbay back that up. Diamond jigs and Deadly Dicks worked fast on the retrieve are taking blues in the 3 to 6-pound class, often mixed right in with the mackerel schools, which makes for a busy rod if you're not paying attention to what just ate your jig.

Speaking of mackerel — that's been the most dependable bite in the zone all week. Eastern Egg Rock and the water around the Cuckolds have both had thick schools working the surface most mornings, easy pickings on mackerel trees or small Swedish pimples jigged fast through 15 to 30 feet of water. It's meat-and-potatoes fishing, but it's produced when the bass have made you wait, and it's also filling coolers with fresh bait for anyone planning to soak eels or chunks for stripers that evening.

Groundfish remain the steadiest hand in the deck right now, and that's not changing anytime soon. Pollock have been stacking up and surface-feeding around Monhegan's White Head ledges most mornings on the last of the incoming tide, chasing bait right up into visible boils — a fast-sinking diamond jig worked with a sweeping retrieve through the top thirty feet has been the go-to, and fish in the 8 to 15-pound class aren't uncommon out there this time of year. Deeper in the bay, cod and a scattering of haddock are still holding in the channels east of Isle au Haut and around Matinicus, 150 to 250 feet of water, taken on bait rigs and heavier jigs bounced right off bottom on the tail end of the drift. It's not a numbers fishery the way it was decades back, but for a boat willing to run the distance and fish it slow and patient on the tide change, there's still enough down there to make the trip worthwhile.

Looking at the next several days, the building moon is the thing to watch. As the tidal flow strengthens through the weekend, expect the bait at the river mouths to organize a little tighter, which usually pulls the bass into shorter, more aggressive feeding windows rather than the lazy, spread-out pattern they've shown lately. If the first real cool nights show up in the back half of September like they typically do, that's the trigger that pushes stripers off the bait schools and into blitz behavior along the outer shorelines and river mouths — worth keeping an eye on overnight temperatures heading into next week. Until then, the mackerel and bluefish are the sure thing inshore, and the pollock at Monhegan and the deep channel cod and haddock around Matinicus and Isle au Haut are the better bet if a boat's looking for something with more backbone than a bay full of staged, unhurried stripers.
